The flexatone is an indirectly struck idiophone that appeared in the early twentieth century, Hornbostel–Sachs 154. A small flexible metal plate is fixed to a metal wire frame with a handle at one end, and beaters of wood or rubber are mounted on both sides. The player holds the frame in one hand, presses and releases the plate with the thumb to change its curvature and pitch, and shakes the handle so that the beaters strike alternately, producing a roll and glissando. It appeared in jazz bands of the 1920s and is also used in orchestras, film and cartoon scores, and in funk and pop to make eerie or sliding effects.
彈音器為20世紀初出現的現代敲擊樂器，1922、1923年見於英國專利記錄，19: The flexatone is a modern percussion instrument of the early twentieth century; it appears in British patent records in 1922 and 1923, and was patented in the United States in 1924 by the Playatone company of New York, the name flex-a-tone referring to the plate's flexing to change pitch. It was at first an effect instrument in jazz bands and later entered the orchestra, used in the second movement of Khachaturian's Piano Concerto; because its intonation is unreliable, most versions give that passage to the first violins instead. Between 1920 and 1970 the word "Flexatone" also meant the musical saw, and it appears in film, cartoon, pop and classical works.
彈音器發聲時帶有尖銳、穿透的滑音與顫音，音色被形容為介於鋸琴的平滑與鐘琴的敲擊感: The flexatone sounds with a sharp, penetrating glissando and tremolo, a timbre described as lying between the smoothness of the musical saw and the struck quality of the glockenspiel. Its range and intonation are limited; pressing the plate with the thumb changes pitch, but specifying an exact pitch is difficult. Volume is controlled by the force with which the handle is shaken, and the dynamic range is not large; compared with instruments of the same group such as the vibraphone, it relies more on shaking and pressing to produce glissandi than on striking a stable pitch with mallets.
演奏者以一手握住金屬支架，手掌環繞框架，拇指置於金屬片自由端；以手腕前後搖動使兩: The player holds the metal frame in one hand with the palm around it and the thumb on the free end of the plate; the wrist shakes back and forth so that the beaters on either side strike alternately, and the thumb presses or releases to change the curvature and pitch, producing a glissando or tremolo. A beginner should first practise steady shaking and control of force, then thumb pressure; because exact pitches are hard, a beginner can aim for approximate pitch at first. If the wooden beaters are removed, a small metal rod can be used to strike it, which is easier to control.
